extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, students of fiction, and literary critics interested in narrative method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on narrative method for novels: how to choose and execute panoramic (pictorial) vs scenic (dramatic) presentation, manage authorial presence/ironies, place characters in their world, and prepare and enact climaxes so the book feels unified and self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial irony / impersonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an ironical, impersonal authorial stance that can supersede a character's limited vision and watch their display 'with a touch of disdain.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that Flaubert's 'irony gives him perfect freedom to supersede [Emma's] limited vision whenever he pleases' and that this impersonality 'artfully operates.' This resource is 'indispensable' when the author needs to move outside a character's view without dislocation—but it must be used with a consistent standard so the switch of perspective feels discreet and coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place characters securely in their social world (multiple perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be shown not only from their own inward view but also as they appear to others — e.g., giving Emma's appearance in the sight of those about her and seeing her from her husband's side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing glimpses of a character from other characters' viewpoints 'makes a more solid figure' for the reader and 'establishes her in the circle of their experience.' This is also practical: if a character (like Charles) will be needed for the climax, his inner mind and point of view 'must be created in advance and kept in reserve' so the climax's force is felt immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and structural unity (well-made book)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the main affair of the novel within another related affair so that the book opens and closes in a balanced way — producing a 'well-made book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madame Bovary is described as 'effectively framed' by Charles's story, which opens and closes the book; framing helps make the whole account compact and complete. The author should marshal material so main action and framing interact to create unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict variety of method to bare needs; scrupulous use of resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the variety of narrative methods and use stylistic resources only to the extent the story requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpt praises a book that has 'variety of method, and with its careful restriction of that variety to its bare needs, and with its scrupulous use of its resources.' Excessive or gratuitous shifts of method dilute effect; every device should serve the story's needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose between panoramic (pictorial) and scenic (dramatic) presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the story is best presented as a broad panorama (surveying a world/society) or as scenic drama (direct enactment of events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The panoramic method (Thackeray) treats the novel as a 'general, typical impression of life,' conveyed in a leisurely, contemplative reminiscence; scenic method requires immediate enactment of crucial events. Choose the method 'which the story means to create'—panorama for impression of manners and society, drama for decisive scenes that must be witnessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic/pictorial technique and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the panoramic method, rely on wide survey, foreshortened detail, reminiscence, and authorial mediation to create an impression of a world rather than isolating single plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristics include: the whole in view at once; 'leisurely, contemplative reminiscence'; drifting into illustrative incidents; 'brief' hints and glimpses rather than continuous scenes. But the panoramic approach may poorly prepare for demanding dramatic climaxes: it can avoid detailed enactment until the last moment, forcing crude devices to produce a climax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic/dramatic enactment for climaxes
rubrics_metrics.description: When the narrative requires a decisive answer or climax, present the event directly and immediately — 'the plain and immediate performance of the answer, its embodiment in a scene that shall pass directly in front of us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpt argues that certain moments (e.g., the collapse of Becky's plotting) must be enacted on stage, not summarized, because 'the force of the answer will be impaired if it is not given with the best possible warrant.' Dramatic scenes supply ocular proof and authoritative evidence that summaries cannot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and reserve characters for later necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: When a character will be needed for a later climactic insight or discovery, create and sustain that character's inner life and point of view in advance so their later role is credible and forceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Charles's inner mind is 'created in advance and kept in reserve' so that when he discovers Emma's faithlessness the climax has full impact. Early episodes that establish a character’s history help make them available for later narrative purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance summary/foreshortening with moments of direct vision
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short, piercing glimpses and foreshortened incidents to enrich a panoramic narrative, but recognize when the material demands a cleared space for direct dramatic vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thackeray's technique often 'drifts into' incidents that 'illustrate what he has to say' with little particularizing, and this can be effective. Yet for certain occasions a brief but decisive presentational shift — 'a space is cleared for it, the stage is swept' — is required to produce dramatic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage narrator's authority and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful of the omniscient narrator's presence: an overt narrative voice can leave the book feeling 'not complete in itself' unless the narrator's point of view is accounted for within the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that when the author flourishes their point of view it may 'draw the eye away from the book itself.' To avoid a sense of an unbounded external authority, either make the narrator's perspective objective and verifiable within the book or integrate the narrator's role into the design so the novel feels self-contained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity through typicality rather than intricate plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: In a panoramic work, the unity of the book may come from the cast of characters being strongly and picturesquely typical of their world, rather than from an intricately woven plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thackeray's Vanity Fair achieves unity because 'all his throng of men and women are strongly, picturesquely typical of the world' and together they 'unite to tell' the story of an age or manners. If unity is achieved by typal representation, avoid forcing dramatic intrigue that obscures the impressionistic aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt method to the author's natural strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize an author's habitual mode (e.g., tendency toward panorama or theater) and avoid forcing techniques that the author cannot naturally sustain, which can lead to awkward or theatrical effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The excerpt notes Thackeray 'was not naturally inclined to the theatre' and when forced into high drama his methods produce a somewhat artificial effect. Authors should choose and prepare for scenes in ways congruent with their narrative temperament to prevent crude devices or 'unnatural effort' at climactic moments.
